{{Short description|Generalization of the Riemann integral}}
{{Use American English|date = March 2019}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Riemann–Stieltjes integral''' is a generalization of the [[Riemann integral]], named after [[Bernhard Riemann]] and [[Thomas Joannes Stieltjes]]. The definition of this integral was first published in 1894 by Stieltjes.{{sfnp|Stieltjes|1894|pp=68–71}} It serves as an instructive and useful precursor of the [[Lebesgue integral]], and an invaluable tool in unifying equivalent forms of statistical theorems that apply to discrete and continuous probability.

==Formal definition==
The Riemann–Stieltjes [[integral]] of a [[real-valued function]] <math>f</math> of a real variable on the interval <math>[a,b]</math> with respect to another real-to-real function <math>g</math> is denoted by

:<math>\int_{x=a}^b f(x) \, \mathrm{d}g(x).</math>

Its definition uses a sequence of [[partition of an interval|partitions]] <math>P</math> of the interval <math>[a,b]</math>

:<math>P=\{ a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n = b\}.</math>

The integral, then, is defined to be the limit, as the [[partition of an interval#Norm of a partition|mesh]] (the length of the longest subinterval) of the partitions approaches <math> 0 </math>, of the approximating sum

:<math>S(P,f,g) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(c_i)\left[ g(x_{i}) - g(x_{i-1}) \right]</math>

where <math>c_i</math> is in the <math>i</math>-th subinterval <math>[x_{i-1},x_{i}]</math>.  The two functions <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are respectively called the ''integrand'' and the ''integrator''. Typically <math>g</math> is taken to be [[Monotonic function|monotone]] (or at least of [[bounded variation]]) and [[Semi-continuity|right-semicontinuous]] (however this last is essentially convention). We specifically do not require <math>g</math> to be continuous, which allows for integrals that have point mass terms.

The "limit" is here understood to be a number ''A'' (the value of the Riemann–Stieltjes integral) such that for every ''ε''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0, there exists ''δ''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 such that for every partition ''P'' with mesh(''P'')&nbsp;<&nbsp;''δ'', and for every choice of points ''c''<sub>''i''</sub> in [''x''<sub>''i''−1</sub>,&nbsp;''x''<sub>''i''</sub>],

:<math>|S(P,f,g)-A| < \varepsilon. \, </math>

==Properties==
The Riemann–Stieltjes integral admits [[integration by parts]] in the form

<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x) \, \mathrm{d}g(x)=f(b)g(b)-f(a)g(a)-\int_a^b g(x) \, \mathrm{d}f(x)</math>

and the existence of either integral implies the existence of the other.{{sfnp|Hille|Phillips|1974|loc=§3.3}}

On the other hand, a classical result{{sfnp|Young|1936}} shows that the integral is well-defined if ''f'' is ''α''-[[Hölder continuous]] and ''g'' is ''β''-Hölder continuous with {{nowrap|''α'' + ''β'' > 1}}&nbsp;.

If <math>f</math> is bounded on <math>[a,b]</math>, <math>g</math> differentiable, monotonically increasing, and <math>g'</math> is Riemann integrable, then the Riemann–Stieltjes integral is related to the Riemann integral by
<math display=block>\int_a^b f(x) \, \mathrm{d}g(x) = \int_a^b f(x) g'(x) \, \mathrm{d}x</math>

For a step function
<math display=block>g(x) = \begin{cases}
	
  0 & \text{if } x \leq s \\
	
  1 & \text{if } x > s \\
	
 \end{cases}</math>	
where <math>a < s < b</math>, if <math>f</math> is continuous at <math>s</math>, then
<math display=block>\int_a^b f(x) \, \mathrm{d}g(x) = f(s)</math>

==Application to probability theory==<!-- This section is linked from [[Probability distribution]] -->

If ''g'' is the [[cumulative distribution function|cumulative probability distribution function]] of a [[random variable]] ''X'' that has a [[probability density function]] with respect to [[Lebesgue measure]], and ''f'' is any function for which the [[expected value]] <math>\operatorname{E}\left[\,\left|f(X)\right|\,\right]</math> is finite, then the probability density function of ''X'' is the derivative of ''g'' and we have

:<math>\operatorname{E}[f(X)]=\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)g'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x.</math>

But this formula does not work if ''X'' does not have a probability density function with respect to Lebesgue measure.  In particular, it does not work if the distribution of ''X'' is discrete (i.e., all of the probability is accounted for by point-masses), and even if the cumulative distribution function ''g'' is continuous, it does not work if ''g'' fails to be [[absolute continuity|absolutely continuous]] (again, the [[Cantor function]] may serve as an example of this failure).  But the identity

:<math>\operatorname{E}[f(X)]=\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\, \mathrm{d}g(x)</math>

holds if ''g'' is ''any'' cumulative probability distribution function on the real line, no matter how ill-behaved.  In particular, no matter how ill-behaved the cumulative distribution function ''g'' of a random variable ''X'', if the [[moment (mathematics)|moment]] E(''X''<sup>''n''</sup>) exists, then it is equal to

: <math>\operatorname{E}\left[X^n\right] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x^n\,\mathrm{d}g(x). </math>

==Application to functional analysis==
The Riemann–Stieltjes integral appears in the original formulation of [[Riesz–Markov–Kakutani representation theorem|F. Riesz's theorem]] which represents  the [[dual space]] of the [[Banach space]]  ''C''[''a'',''b''] of continuous functions in an interval [''a'',''b''] as Riemann–Stieltjes integrals against functions of [[bounded variation]].  Later, that theorem was reformulated in terms of measures.

The Riemann–Stieltjes integral also appears in the formulation of the [[spectral theorem]] for (non-compact) self-adjoint (or more generally, normal) operators in a Hilbert space.  In this theorem, the integral is considered with respect to a spectral family of projections.<ref>See {{harvp|Riesz|Sz. Nagy|1990}} for details.</ref>

==Existence of the integral==
The best simple existence theorem states that if ''f'' is continuous and ''g'' is of [[bounded variation]] on [''a'', ''b''], then the integral exists.{{sfnp|Johnsonbaugh|Pfaffenberger|2010|p=219}}{{sfnp|Rudin|1964|pp=121–122}}{{sfnp|Kolmogorov|Fomin|1975|p=368}}
Because of the integration by part formula, the integral exists also if the condition on ''f'' and ''g'' are inversed, that is, if ''f'' is of bounded variation and ''g'' is continuous. 

A function ''g'' is of bounded variation if and only if it is the difference between two (bounded) monotone functions.  If ''g'' is not of bounded variation, then there will be continuous functions which cannot be integrated with respect to ''g''.  In general, the integral is not well-defined if ''f'' and ''g'' share any points of [[Discontinuity (mathematics)|discontinuity]], but there are other cases as well.

==Geometric interpretation==
A 3D plot, with ''x'', ''f(x)'', and ''g(x)'' all along orthogonal axes, leads to a geometric interpretation of the Riemann–Stieltjes integral.<ref>{{harvp|Bullock|1988}}</ref> [[File:Basic geometry of riemann-stieljes integral f g x.png|thumb|right|500x600px|The basic geometry of the Riemann-Stieltjes integral.]] If the ''g(x)-x'' plane is horizontal and the ''f(x)''-direction is pointing upward, then the surface to be considered is like a curved fence. The fence follows the curve traced by ''g(x)'', and the height of the fence is given by ''f(x)''. The fence is the section of the ''g(x)''-sheet (i.e., the ''g(x)'' curve extended along the ''f(x)'' axis) that is bounded between the ''g(x)-x'' plane and the ''f(x)''-sheet. The Riemann-Stieltjes integral is the area of the projection of this fence onto the ''f(x)-g(x)'' plane &mdash; in effect, its "shadow".

The slope of ''g(x)'' weights the area of the projection. The values of ''x'' for which ''g(x)'' has the steepest slope ''g'(x)'' correspond to regions of the fence with the greater projection and thereby carry the most weight in the integral. [[File:Curvature effects on geometry of riemann-stieljes integral f g x.png|thumb|right|500x600px|The effects of curvature in ''g(x)'' on the geometry of the Riemann-Stieltjes integral.]]

When ''g'' is a step function
<math display=block>g(x) = \begin{cases}
  0 & \text{if } x \leq s \\
  1 & \text{if } x > s \\
 \end{cases}</math>
the fence has a rectangular "gate" of width 1 and height equal to ''f(s)''. Thus the gate, and its projection, have area equal to ''f(s)'', the value of the Riemann-Stieltjes integral. [[File:Step function effect on geometry of riemann-stieljes integral f g x.png|thumb|right|500x200px|The effect of a step function <math>g(x)</math> on the geometry of the Riemann-Stieltjes integral.]]

==Generalization==
An important generalization is the [[Lebesgue&ndash;Stieltjes integral]], which generalizes the Riemann–Stieltjes integral in a way analogous to how the [[Lebesgue integral]] generalizes the Riemann integral. If [[improper integral|improper]] Riemann–Stieltjes integrals are allowed, then the Lebesgue integral is not strictly more general than the Riemann–Stieltjes integral.

The Riemann–Stieltjes integral also generalizes{{citation needed|date=March 2019}} to the case when either the integrand ''ƒ'' or the integrator ''g'' take values in a [[Banach space]].  If {{nowrap|''g'' : [''a'',''b''] &rarr; ''X''}} takes values in the Banach space ''X'', then it is natural to assume that it is of '''strongly bounded variation''', meaning that

:<math>\sup \sum_i {\| g(t_{i-1})-g(t_i) \|}_X < \infty </math>
the supremum being taken over all finite partitions
:<math>a=t_0\le t_1\le\cdots\le t_n=b</math>
of the interval [''a'',''b''].  This generalization plays a role in the study of [[c0-semigroup|semigroups]], via the [[Laplace–Stieltjes transform]].

The [[Itô calculus|Itô integral]] extends the Riemann–Stietjes integral to encompass integrands and integrators which are [[stochastic process]]es rather than simple functions; see also [[stochastic calculus]].

===Generalized Riemann–Stieltjes integral===
A slight generalization<ref>Introduced by {{harvp|Pollard|1920}} and now standard in analysis.</ref> is to consider in the above definition partitions ''P'' that ''refine'' another partition ''P''<sub>''ε''</sub>, meaning that ''P'' arises from ''P''<sub>''ε''</sub> by the addition of points, rather than from partitions with a finer mesh. Specifically, the '''generalized Riemann–Stieltjes integral''' of ''f'' with respect to ''g'' is a number ''A'' such that for every ''ε''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 there exists a partition ''P''<sub>''ε''</sub> such that for every partition ''P'' that refines ''P''<sub>''ε''</sub>,

:<math>|S(P,f,g) - A| < \varepsilon \, </math>

for every choice of points ''c''<sub>''i''</sub> in [''x''<sub>''i''</sub>,&nbsp;''x''<sub>''i''+1</sub>].

This generalization exhibits the Riemann–Stieltjes integral as the [[Moore–Smith limit]] on the [[directed set]] of partitions of [''a'',&nbsp;''b'']&nbsp;.{{sfnp|McShane|1952}}<ref>{{harvp|Hildebrandt|1938}} calls it  the '''Pollard–Moore–Stieltjes integral'''.</ref>

A consequence is that with this definition, the integral <math display="inline"> \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}g(x) </math> can still be defined in cases where ''f'' and ''g'' have a point of discontinuity in common.

===Darboux sums===
The Riemann–Stieltjes integral can be efficiently handled using an appropriate generalization of [[Darboux sum]]s.  For a partition ''P'' and a nondecreasing function ''g'' on [''a'',&nbsp;''b''] define the upper Darboux sum of ''f'' with respect to ''g'' by

<math display="block">U(P,f,g) = \sum_{i=1}^n \,\, [\,g(x_i)-g(x_{i-1})\,] \,\sup_{x\in [x_{i-1},x_i]} f(x)</math>

and the lower sum by

<math display="block">L(P,f,g) = \sum_{i=1}^n \,\, [\,g(x_i)-g(x_{i-1})\,] \,\inf_{x\in [x_{i-1},x_i]} f(x).</math>

Then the generalized Riemann–Stieltjes of ''f'' with respect to ''g'' exists if and only if, for every ε&nbsp;>&nbsp;0, there exists a partition ''P'' such that

:<math>U(P,f,g)-L(P,f,g) < \varepsilon.</math>

Furthermore, ''f'' is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable with respect to ''g'' (in the classical sense) if

:<math>\lim_{\operatorname{mesh}(P)\to 0} [\,U(P,f,g)-L(P,f,g)\,] = 0.\quad</math>{{sfnp|Graves|1946|loc=Chap. XII, §3}}

==Examples and special cases==
=== Differentiable ''g'' ===
Given a <math>g(x)</math> which is continuously [[Differentiable function|differentiable]] over <math>\mathbb{R}</math> it can be shown that there is the equality
Let <math>g</math> be continuously differentiable on <math>\mathbb{R}</math>. Then,
:<math>
\int_a^b f(x) \, \mathrm{d}g(x) = \int_a^b f(x)g'(x) \, \mathrm{d}x
</math>
where the integral on the right-hand side is the standard Riemann integral, assuming that <math>f</math> can be integrated by the Riemann–Stieltjes integral.

More generally, the Riemann integral equals the Riemann–Stieltjes integral if <math>g</math> is the [[Lebesgue integral]] of its derivative; in this case <math>g</math> is said to be [[absolutely continuous]].

It may be the case that <math>g</math> has jump discontinuities, or may have derivative zero ''almost'' everywhere while still being continuous and increasing (for example, <math>g</math> could be the [[Cantor function]] or “Devil's staircase”), in either of which cases the Riemann–Stieltjes integral is not captured by any expression involving derivatives of ''g''.

=== Riemann integral ===
The standard Riemann integral is a special case of the Riemann–Stieltjes integral where <math>g(x) = x</math>.

=== Rectifier ===
Consider the function <math>g(x) = \max\{ 0, x \}</math> used in the study of [[neural network]]s, called a [[Rectifier (neural networks)|''rectified linear unit'' (ReLU)]]. Then the Riemann–Stieltjes can be evaluated as
:<math>
\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}g(x) = \int_{g(a)}^{g(b)}f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x
</math>
where the integral on the right-hand side is the standard Riemann integral.

===Cavalieri integration===
[[File:Riemann–Stieltjes integral.png|thumb|right|434x434px|Visualisation of the Cavalieri integral for the function <math>f(x)=(2x+8)^3</math>]] 
[[Cavalieri's principle]] can be used to calculate areas bounded by curves using Riemann–Stieltjes integrals.<ref>T. L. Grobler, E. R. Ackermann, A. J. van Zyl & J. C. Olivier 
[http://researchspace.csir.co.za/dspace/bitstream/handle/10204/5267/Grobler5_2011.pdf;jsessionid=C0A9818B6A46CA5AD17AD91DFD982F3A?sequence=1 Cavalieri integration] from [[Council for Scientific and Industrial Research]]</ref> The integration strips of Riemann integration are replaced with strips that are non-rectangular in shape. The method is to transform a "Cavalieri region" with a transformation <math>h</math>, or to use <math>g = h^{-1}</math> as integrand.

For a given function <math>f(x)</math> on an interval <math>[a,b]</math>, a "translational function" <math>a(y)</math> must intersect <math>(x,f(x ))</math> exactly once for any shift in the interval. A "Cavalieri region" is then bounded by  <math>f(x),a(y)</math>, the <math>x</math>-axis, and <math>b(y) = a(y) + (b-a)</math>. The area of the region is then
:<math>\int_{a(y)}^{b(y)} f(x) \, dx \ = \ \int_{a'}^{b'} f(x) \, dg(x) ,</math>
where <math>a'</math> and <math>b'</math> are the <math>x</math>-values where  <math>a(y)</math> and  <math>b(y)</math> intersect <math>f(x)</math>.
